User: Summarize the importance of preserving family narratives according to Jim Ison and the research he quoted.: Ever frighten yourself when you couldn’t recall a family story or experiences you know had to have been recounted to you many times by your grandparents? Ever wonder why you know very little about the personal lives of your grandparents or great-grandparents?
Jim Ison, an area manager for FamilySearch.org and a recent luncheon speaker at the National Genealogical Society’s 2014 conference in Richmond, Virginia, said the notion that his family’s narratives could be lost in three generations gave him the resolve to ensure that didn’t happen on his watch.
Ison thought, “No one knows (my ancestors) like me or their stories that I know. I’m the connecting link between my grandchildren and my grandparents.” He decided at that moment in 2013 to put aside his passion for genealogical research and a long-term goal to trace his genealogy to the great Charlemagne, and instead he began focusing on the rich personal accounts of his parents and grandparents—things he thought his great-grandchildren would want to know and wish he had taken the time to do.
To start out on his new quest, Ison picked a particular set of grandparents to start with, Lorilla Spencer and Frank (Reight) Ison. He scanned their photos and uploaded them to his free FamilySearch.org account and added other source documents he had amassed over the years from his research. He then edited and added stories his father had written about his grandparents years before, and he preserved and shared them online through FamilySearch’s Family Tree.
Ison quoted research from a 2013 New York Times article by author Bruce Feiler, who observed, “The single most important thing you can do for your family may be the simplest of all: develop a strong family narrative.” The research noted that children who knew the most about their forbearers—who they were, where they grew up, illnesses they struggled with, and tough trials they went through, had the greatest self-confidence and dealt with personal stress better.
For posterity’s sake, Ison focused on pointing out such highlights of the personal lives of the ancestors he knew and discovered through research.
For example, his Bavarian grandpa’s mother died when he was a young child. His great-grandfather remarried a “wicked stepmother,” who spanked them every morning and told them the spanking was for anything during the day she wouldn’t catch them doing! This grandfather and his older brother eventually ran away and changed their last name to avoid capture. They immigrated to the United States, worked hard, and were very successful.
His grandmother became a school teacher at a very young age. She was traumatized when her fiancé was killed in a tragic accident. To escape the constant reminder in the local community of her heartache, she applied to teach in Alaska and was rejected ironically because she wasn’t married. She applied in Georgia and was refused because she was a “Yankee” from South Dakota. She applied in Kentucky and was accepted, which explained why she was willing to relocate 1,300 miles on horseback on her own, without the comforts of home and family.
As a newly married couple, the home of these same grandparents’ burnt down.
Ison created questions from the stories and photos for these two grandparents, Frank and Lorilla, that would entice his grandchildren to know more about their fascinating great-grandparents.
At age 9, why did Frank leave home with his brother?
What did he do in the United States while in the German Navy?
Who was responsible for him changing his last name from “Rieght” to “Ison”?
How old was Lorilla when she started teaching?
Why did she move 1,300 miles from South Dakota to Kentucky?
Ison said he marveled at how enthralled his grandkids have been in looking for the answers in the photos and stories he published online at FamilySearch.org and how easily they navigated the online tools to do so.
Ison is now moving on to repeat the process for other grandparents and ancestors in his tree, very content in his new role as the intergenerational connection for his posterity.

He believes that children who know about their forbearers' lives and experiences have greater self-confidence and resilience to deal with personal stress. Ison himself decided to focus on his grandparents' rich personal histories and stories so that they are not lost in three generations. He trained his focus on his grandparents Lorilla Spencer and Frank (Reight) Ison and added their photos and source documents to his free FamilySearch.org account. He quoted a 2013 New York Times article by Bruce Feiler that "the single most important thing you can do for your family may be the simplest of all: develop a strong family narrative." Ison created questions from the stories and photos of his grandparents to entice his grandchildren to learn more about their great-grandparents. He is content in his new role as the link between his grandparents and great-grandchildren.
User: Can you provide me with more information on the benefits of children knowing about their ancestors' personal experiences?
Assistant: Research has shown that children who know about their ancestors' personal experiences have a greater sense of self and identity. They have greater resilience in the face of difficulties because they know that their ancestors overcame similar or even greater obstacles. It also helps them understand their family's history and culture, giving them a sense of belonging and connection to their family's legacy. This understanding can improve communication and relationships among family members as well. Knowing about their ancestors' life experiences and struggles can also provide children with examples of perseverance, courage, and resilience, inspiring them to overcome their own challenges. All in all, preserving family narratives and personal accounts of ancestors can have a significant positive impact on children's emotional wellbeing and personality development.
User: Can you suggest some specific ways to preserve family narratives and personal accounts of ancestors based on the examples shared by Jim Ison?
Assistant: Yes, based on Jim Ison's examples, here are some specific ways to preserve family narratives and personal accounts of ancestors:

1. Start by selecting a particular set of grandparents or great-grandparents whose personal stories you want to preserve. 

2. Gather as many photographs, documents (such as letters, diaries, and other written records), and other memorabilia as you can from your family members. 

3. Use online resources like FamilySearch.org to create a family tree and upload the photos and documents you have collected. 

4. Edit and add any stories you or other family members have written or recorded to the family tree. 

5. Create questions from the stories and photos of your ancestors, similar to how Jim Ison did, to entice younger generations to learn more about their great-grandparents.

6. Share the stories and photos with your family members online or at family gatherings. 

7. Consider making a scrapbook or a family history book with photos and stories to pass down to future generations. 

8. Encourage other family members to contribute their own stories and photos to the family tree or scrapbook, to create a more complete picture of your family's history. 

By following these steps, you can help ensure that your family's personal accounts and narratives are preserved and appreciated by future generations.
User: Can you provide more examples of questions that can be created from the stories and photos of ancestors, similar to what Jim Ison did?
Assistant: Sure, here are some more examples of questions that can be created from the stories and photos of ancestors to entice younger generations to learn more:

2. How did your great-grandparents meet, and what was their courtship like?

3. What challenges did your ancestors face when immigrating to America or moving to a new area, and how did they overcome them?

4. What were some of your ancestors' proudest achievements or moments, and what made those experiences so special to them?

5. What were some of the hardest times your ancestors faced, and what did they do to persevere through those challenges?

6. What were some of the values that your ancestors held most dear, and how did they pass those values on to their children and grandchildren?

7. What family traditions or customs did your ancestors observe, and how did those traditions evolve over time?

8. What talents or unique skills did your ancestors possess, and how did they use those skills to benefit their families and communities?

These are just a few examples of many possible questions that can be created from the stories and photos of ancestors. By asking open-ended, curious questions like these, you can encourage younger generations to connect with their family's history and to appreciate the experiences and accomplishments of their ancestors.
